summary: A guide for people running or starting a Network Information Center, network operations centers, and the agencies that fund them. It describes how to build an information service infrastructure to help Internet users. It is an informational FYI document.

eli5.summary: A how-to book for running a help desk for the Internet. It explains how to set one up so people can find answers and get help.

questions: how to build a network information center

subtitle: A blueprint for Internet help desks and information centers

tldr.problem: As the Internet grew in the 1980s and 1990s, individual networks needed a way to help users understand how to connect and use these growing resources, and to coordinate information and support across different networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines Network Information Centers (NICs) as organizations providing information, administrative support, and help to users, and establishes four essential functions they should perform: providing information resources, supporting end-users directly, collecting referral information about other NICs, and supporting the NIC infrastructure itself.
tldr.outcome: This became a foundational model for Internet user support, with NICs established by major networks like NSF, Energy Science, and NASA, though the role has evolved with the Web and decentralized information sources.

facts.label: Major networks with NICs
facts.value: MILNET, NSFNET, ESnet, NASA Science Internet

today: RFC 1302 defined the role of Network Information Centers and the services they should provide. The specific model—telephone and email hotlines, FTP repositories, and central NICs—evolved as the Web and search engines became the dominant way people found information. However, the underlying principles remain: user support, coordinated information services, and security awareness continue to be essential to network operations.

sections.title: What NICs Are and Why They Matter
sections.content:
A Network Information Center (NIC) is an organization that helps users understand and use a network. When the ARPANET was created in the 1970s, SRI took on this role by maintaining the host registry and keeping copies of technical documents, answering user calls, and becoming a central place where people could find help. As the Internet grew into thousands of networks, each network needed its own NIC to serve local users and to coordinate with NICs serving other networks.

This RFC was written by the Network Information Services Infrastructure working group to define what all Internet NICs should do. It treats the NIC as separate from a Network Operations Center (NOC), which handles the technical running of the network itself. A NIC focuses on serving users and providing information.
sections.eli5: When the early Internet was small, one organization kept track of all the computers and answered questions. As it grew, every big network needed its own help desk. This document explains what a good help desk should do.

sections.title: The Four Essential Functions
sections.content:
The RFC identifies four main things every Internet NIC should do. First, provide information resources: this means making documents, newsletters, and other information available online or in print, as well as knowing where information is stored on other networks and referring users there. Each piece of information should include a timestamp, a version number, and the name of the NIC that created it, so users know how current and authoritative it is.

Second, support end-users directly through telephone hotlines and email addresses. The NIC should take responsibility for each user inquiry until it is resolved—either by answering it, referring the user to the right place, or working with the Network Operations Center on technical problems. The RFC suggests a standard email address format: NIC@domain (for example, NIC@NSF.NET), so users know where to ask for help.

Third, collect and maintain NIC referral information. With so many networks and NICs, no single NIC can know everything. The RFC proposes a database called nic-profiles where each NIC records its areas of expertise and resources, so every NIC can route users to the right place. Fourth, support the NIC infrastructure by participating in the IETF User Services Working Group and joining a mailing list called nic-forum where NIC staff can share solutions to common problems and post information of interest.
sections.eli5: Every help desk needs to do four things: keep good information available, answer questions from people who call or email, know about other help desks and what they do, and work together with other help desks to get better.

sections.title: Services NICs Provide in Practice
sections.content:
The RFC describes the kinds of services that NICs actually offered in the early 1990s. Direct user support included making referrals to other resources, setting up user-to-user communication through electronic conferences or mailing lists, offering support for specific applications, providing technical expertise to troubleshoot problems, and sending emergency notices when outages or security events could affect users.

Training services included seminars and workshops ranging from "what is the Internet" to specialized classes on supercomputer applications. Marketing and public relations involved publishing newsletters, producing how-to guides and brochures, and writing press releases. Information repositories stored online files and made them available for download, and administrative services included registering users in white pages databases, keeping records of hosts and networks, and maintaining contact information.
sections.eli5: NICs helped in lots of ways: they answered questions, taught classes, published newsletters, kept files for download, kept databases of who is who, and sometimes set up online discussion groups.

sections.title: How Information Reaches Users
sections.content: The RFC documents thirteen mechanisms NICs used in the early 1990s to reach users. Electronic mail was used for general information, newsletters, and security alerts. File Transfer Protocol (FTP) allowed users to download network maps, technical specifications, drafts of RFCs, and any file-based information. Telephone hotlines provided answers to specific questions and help with connecting. Hard copy (printed materials) delivered newsletters and guides by postal mail. Presentations and seminars reached groups of users to explain technologies and share trends. Remote systems and Telnet provided access to applications and databases. Electronic bulletin boards and electronic conferences let users read and post messages. Directory services like Finger and Whois looked up user information. The RFC notes that the most effective NICs used multiple methods, choosing the best delivery method for each type of information.
sections.eli5: NICs sent information in lots of different ways: email, file downloads, phone calls, printed mail, classes, and bulletin boards where users could read and post messages. Different information went different ways depending on what users needed.

sections.title: Keeping Information Accurate and Secure
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that NICs often maintain databases of important information—user records, host information, contact details—and gives recommendations for how to handle these responsibly. When collecting data for a database, NICs should disclose to users why the information is being collected, what will be done with it, which fields are required and which optional, which information will be public, how to update it, and how often updates will be requested. Users should know when their personal information is in a public database and have the opportunity to correct or remove it.

The RFC also addresses security awareness. NICs interact directly with users and sometimes with security incidents. The RFC recommends that NICs know which agencies and groups handle Internet security incidents, be aware of security mailing lists and resources (citing the Site Security Handbook, RFC 1244), advocate for security practices to users, and have explicit procedures in place for responding to security incidents, including coordination with response centers and the NOC.
sections.eli5: When a NIC keeps a database of information about people, it needs to tell them what's being kept, ask permission to share it, let them change it, and keep it safe. NICs should also know how to handle security emergencies and help users stay secure.
